Files: logistics/access.py (can_pass), logistics/routes.py (passable_route, rerouted_sites), notifications/sms.py (notify_rerouted), distribution/planner.py (use passable_route so deliveries don't use blocked roads). Also maybe a test? No, tests read-only.

can_pass semantics: R11 says docstring says both R and X closed to all vehicles. But ticket says "given the road's current status code" and vehicle truck/van. The ask: can_pass(road_id, vehicle) -> bool whether vehicle may use road given status. Per docstring, only "A" allows. But VEHICLE_WEIGHT exists... R11 warns no light-vehicle exception documented. So safest: can_pass returns status == OPEN for both vehicles? Hmm, but then "sending a truck if a truck may use every road and a van otherwise" — van would never differ. But we must rely only on findings. R11 explicitly says under documented rules no vehicle may pass non-"A" road. So can_pass: return road_status(road_id, network) == OPEN, regardless of vehicle. Actually maybe use VEHICLE_WEIGHT? The findings don't state any rule differentiating. So implement: status == OPEN.

Hmm, but then passable_route: route usable if at least one vehicle may use every road — same as all roads open. Vehicle = truck if truck can use every road else van. With can_pass same for both, vehicle always truck. That's fine per findings.

Wait — but maybe restricted roads allow vans? The docstring says R = "restricted: closed to all vehicles until the road is cleared". So no. Follow R11.

Actually, could interpret: can_pass uses VEHICLE_WEIGHT to check... no documented rule. Keep it simple: passable iff status == OPEN. But then why vehicle param? Just accept it. I'll write can_pass to check status == OPEN (per docstring semantics in R1/R11), for either vehicle.

Hmm, but "Done when: trucks are sent whenever the route allows it" — with all-or-nothing, truck always when route passable. Fine.

Alternatively, maybe plan can_pass as: OPEN → True for all; RESTRICTED/CLOSED → False. Yes.

P2: logistics/routes.py — add passable_route(warehouse_id, site, network=None). For each route from routes_between, check can_pass for each road; usable if any vehicle passes all roads (truck first). Return (route, "truck") if truck passes all roads, else (route, "van") if van passes all, pick shortest by (km, id) like best_route (R3). Return None if none. uses R2, R3, after P1.

P3: logistics/routes.py — add rerouted_sites(network=None): iterate sites (sites_served per warehouse? Hmm — rerouted_sites needs sites across warehouses). We don't know warehouse ids from findings except examples WH-NVL-03, WH-CPL-05, WH-HGL-07. We can't invent a warehouse list... but network.json presumably has warehouses. Findings don't state network structure beyond routes and roads. Hmm.

Option: rerouted_sites iterates over all sites — could derive from network["routes"] unique "to" values, sorted. That's like sites_served but without warehouse filter. But R10 says sites_served(warehouse_id) returns sorted unique sites with a route from the warehouse. We could get warehouses from network... unknown key. Safer: collect unique r["to"] across network["routes"], sorted — reuse pattern. Or: for each route in network["routes"], site = r["to"]. I'll say: gather the set of sites from network["routes"] (r["to"]), sorted; for each site, compare passable_route(warehouse, site) vs best_route(warehouse, site) using the warehouse from the route record (r["from"]). Actually each site may have routes from multiple warehouses; compare per (warehouse, site) pair. Simpler: for each unique (from, to) pair in network["routes"], compare best_route vs passable_route; collect sites where routes differ (route ids differ — "the vehicle alone changing does not count", so compare route identity, e.g. route["id"]). Return sorted unique site names.

uses R3, R10; after P2.
